pages.transcription:
c/o Viking Press
18 East 48th Street
Newyork.                                Newyork, 31st January 1941.

Dear Hanna and Manfred,

My wife has written you that we have finally
settled Eva, and I believe that the whole matter will be arranged to
your entire satisfaction. In the school she will have plenty of
company and of Mrs. Schaeffer, in whose home she is going to live,
we have an excellent impression.
Now the material side of the matter. Thanks
to the generosity of Mr. Salmon where she has been living until now
you have been up to now in the privileged position not to have had
to ask the Treasury for any permission of sending your child money
for nearly six months. Also now the expenses will be nearly com-
pletely covered through reduced fees and through relatives. It will
be only necessary for you to ask permission for the transfer of a
limited amount for smaller expenses, for books, dresses, shoes,
luncheon money, fares, stamps etc. as we would not like to ask our
relatives here also for those things; you know they have plenty of
other obligations. We have been informed that such trifling sums
for the extra expenses have been granted to the parents of British
children over here, and I would advise you to make an application
for such additional monthly contributions. I can assure you that
the school as well as her new home are run on very simple lines, but
nevertheless you know that there are always a number of small extras
to be paid. If you get permission for such a transfer, the money
should be sent directly to Eva's new home, Mrs. A. Schaeffer, Amity
Hall, Mount Airy Road, Croton-on-Hudson, New York.
We are alright here. We have had a good rest
after that exhausting journey, and I have now taken up my work again,
happy to be quietly in my room without any social obligations for the
time being.

Warmest regards

Stefan Zweig
